claims.claim: pFNsyn-bound α5β1 integrins fail to organize functional adhesion sites and to induce contractile stress fibers required for cell spreading.
claims.source: which altogether suggests that pFNsyn-bound α5β1 integrins fail to organize functional adhesion sites and to induce contractile stress fibers required for cell spreading.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the reduced FA formation and spreading data in pKO-β1 cells on pFNsyn.

claims.claim: pKO-αv cells adhere and spread similarly on pFNwt and pFNsyn.
claims.source: pKO-αv cells adhered and spread similarly on pFNwt and pFNsyn, and developed comparably large, paxillin-positive FAs that were anchored to thick stress fibers (Figure 4B,D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4B,D.

claims.claim: pKO-αv/β1 cells show the same adhesion and spreading behavior, and develop similar adhesion sites on pFNsyn, indicating that αv-containing integrins compensate for the absence of a functional synergy site.
claims.source: Importantly, pKO-αv/β1 cells also showed the same adhesion and spreading behavior, and developed similar adhesion sites on pFNsyn indicating that αv-containing integrins compensate for the absence of a functional synergy site (Figure 4B,E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4B,E.

claims.claim: On FNIII7-10wt, pKO-αv and pKO-αv/β1 cells show a 3-fold higher binding probability compared to pKO-β1 cells.
claims.source: On FNIII7-10wt, the experiments revealed a 3-fold higher binding probability of pKO-αv and pKO-αv/β1 cells compared to pKO-β1 cells, indicating that αvβ3 integrins have a higher affinity for FN-RGD than α5β1 integrins.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by single-cell force spectroscopy data.

claims.claim: αvβ3 integrins have a higher affinity for FN-RGD than α5β1 integrins.
claims.source: On FNIII7-10wt, the experiments revealed a 3-fold higher binding probability of pKO-αv and pKO-αv/β1 cells compared to pKO-β1 cells, indicating that αvβ3 integrins have a higher affinity for FN-RGD than α5β1 integrins.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the binding probability data from single-cell force spectroscopy.

claims.claim: Full-length pFN shows higher binding probability than fragments for all cell lines tested including the pKO cells that lack integrin expression.
claims.source: Interestingly, however, full-length pFN showed higher binding probability than fragments for all cell lines tested including the pKO cells that lack integrin expression
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by single-cell force spectroscopy data comparing full-length FN to fragments.

claims.claim: In addition to integrins, other FN-binding cell surface receptor(s) contribute to the initial binding.
claims.source: which altogether suggests that in addition to integrins also other FN-binding cell surface receptor(s) contribute to the initial binding.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the observation that integrin-null pKO cells still show binding to full-length FN.

claims.claim: The FN synergy site promotes the maturation of FAs but accelerates neither the rates of FN binding to α5β1 integrins nor the formation of NAs.
claims.source: These findings indicate that the FN synergy site promotes the maturation of FAs but accelerates neither the rates of FN binding to α5β1 integrins nor the formation of NAs.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the single-cell force spectroscopy and focal adhesion data.

claims.claim: Around 87% of Itgb3-null mice are born and around 40% of them survive the first year of life.
claims.source: Itgb3-null mice fail to express the widely expressed αvβ3 integrins and the platelet-specific αIIbβ3 integrin, and suffer from a bleeding disorder resembling human Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Around 87% of Itgb3-null mice are born and around 40% of them survive the first year of life (Hodivala-Dilke et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to prior work (Hodivala-Dilke et al., 1999).

claims.claim: One instead of the expected 38 compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- mice survived to P21 out of 335 offspring.
claims.source: Out of the 335 offspring altogether, one instead of the expected 38 compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- mice survived to P21.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by breeding data in Table 1.

claims.claim: The single surviving Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- mouse died at the age of 5 months from excessive bleeding.
claims.source: The survivor died at the age of 5 months from excessive bleeding.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation from the breeding experiments.

claims.claim: Compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were present at the expected Mendelian distribution until E15.5.
claims.source: While compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were present at the expected Mendelian distribution until E15.5, no live embryos were present at E16.5 or later.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by embryo genotyping data in Table 1.

claims.claim: No live Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were present at E16.5 or later.
claims.source: While compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were present at the expected Mendelian distribution until E15.5, no live embryos were present at E16.5 or later.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by embryo genotyping data in Table 1.

claims.claim: Mice with one wild-type Itgb3 allele (Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/+) were normally distributed.
claims.source: Interestingly, mice with one wild-type Itgb3 allele (Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/+) were normally distributed, which altogether indicates that one β3 integrin allele is sufficient to compensate for normal development.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by breeding data in Table 1.

claims.claim: One β3 integrin allele is sufficient to compensate for normal development in the context of the Fn1syn mutation.
claims.source: Interestingly, mice with one wild-type Itgb3 allele (Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/+) were normally distributed, which altogether indicates that one β3 integrin allele is sufficient to compensate for normal development.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the normal distribution of Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/+ mice.

claims.claim: Compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos display multiple cutaneous hemorrhages and edema, first visible at E11.5/12.5.
claims.source: Compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos displayed multiple cutaneous hemorrhages and edema, which were first visible at E11.5/12.5 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and then spread over the whole body at E15.5 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by embryo images in Figure 5A, Figure 5B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Lyve1-positive lymphatic vessels in the skin of Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos are dilated and covered with ectopic α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA)-positive cells and filled with Ter119-positive erythroblasts.
claims.source: In line with our hypothesis, Lyve1-positive lymphatic vessels in the skin of Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were dilated and covered with ectopic α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA)-positive cells and filled with Ter119-positive erythroblasts (Figure 5C–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 5C–E.

claims.claim: Lymphatic vessels in the skin of Itgb3-null or wild-type littermates neither contain Ter119-positive cells nor are surrounded with α-smooth muscle actin-positive cells.
claims.source: In contrast, lymphatic vessels in the skin of Itgb3-null or wild-type littermates neither contained Ter119-positive cells nor were surrounded with α-smooth muscle actin-positive cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data showing normal lymphatic vessels in control embryos.

claims.claim: The mean spreading area of wild-type platelets seeded for 60 min on fibrinogen, pFNwt, and pFNsyn is 15–16 μm2.
claims.source: The mean spreading area of wild-type platelets seeded for 60 min on fibrinogen, pFNwt, and pFNsyn was 15–16 μm2.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by platelet spreading assay data.

claims.claim: Itgb3-/- platelets fail to spread on fibrinogen (mean spreading area of 4.6 μm2).
claims.source: As expected, Itgb3-/- platelets failed to spread on fibrinogen (mean spreading area of 4.6 μm2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by platelet spreading assay data.

claims.claim: Itgb3-/- platelets show a reduced mean spreading area of 8.9 μm2 on pFNwt.
claims.source: Furthermore, they showed a reduced mean spreading area of 8.9 μm2 on pFNwt and failed to spread on pFNsyn (mean spreading area of 3.8 μm2) (Figure 6B,C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by platelet spreading assay data in Figure 6B,C.

claims.claim: Itgb3-/- platelets fail to spread on pFNsyn (mean spreading area of 3.8 μm2).
claims.source: Furthermore, they showed a reduced mean spreading area of 8.9 μm2 on pFNwt and failed to spread on pFNsyn (mean spreading area of 3.8 μm2) (Figure 6B,C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by platelet spreading assay data in Figure 6B,C.

claims.claim: Application of shear flow reduces adhesion of wild-type platelets to pFNsyn by 10-fold compared to pFNwt.
claims.source: Application of shear flow reduced adhesion of wild-type platelets to pFNsyn by 10-fold compared to pFNwt, while adhesion of Itgb3-null platelets was lost on fibrinogen as well as pFNsyn, and only slightly diminished on pFNwt (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by flow chamber assay data in Figure 6D,E.

claims.claim: Adhesion of Itgb3-null platelets is lost on fibrinogen and pFNsyn under shear flow.
claims.source: Application of shear flow reduced adhesion of wild-type platelets to pFNsyn by 10-fold compared to pFNwt, while adhesion of Itgb3-null platelets was lost on fibrinogen as well as pFNsyn, and only slightly diminished on pFNwt (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by flow chamber assay data in Figure 6D,E.

claims.claim: Adhesion and spreading of platelets isolated from Itgb3-/- mice to collagen are unaffected, irrespective of whether shear flow is applied or not.
claims.source: Importantly, adhesion and spreading of platelets isolated from Itgb3-/- mice to collagen were unaffected, irrespective of whether shear flow was applied or not (Figure 6C,E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by platelet adhesion and spreading data on collagen in Figure 6C,E.

claims.claim: Adhesion of αIIbβ3-deficient platelets to wild-type FN is partially compensated by α5β1 integrins in a FN synergy site-dependent manner.
claims.source: These in vitro experiments demonstrate that adhesion of αIIbβ3-deficient platelets to wild-type FN is partially compensated by α5β1 integrins in a FN synergy site-dependent manner
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the platelet adhesion and spreading data comparing Itgb3-/- platelets on pFNwt vs pFNsyn.

claims.claim: α5β1 and αIIbβ3 integrins require the FN synergy site for stabilizing platelet adhesion to FN under shear flow.
claims.source: and that α5β1 as well as αIIbβ3 integrins require the FN synergy site for stabilizing platelet adhesion to FN, under shear flow.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the flow chamber assay data showing reduced platelet adhesion on pFNsyn under shear flow.

claims.claim: The arteries and veins of the dermal vasculature of E15.5 Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos are tortuous and irregularly covered with α-SMA-positive cells.
claims.source: While immunostaining of E11.5 whole mount embryos with an anti-PECAM-1 antibody revealed that the vessels in the trunk of Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos showed normal sprouting (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), the arteries and veins of the dermal vasculature of E15.5 embryos were tortuous and irregularly covered with α-SMA-positive cells (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The vascular network has significantly fewer branching points in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos compared to wild-type littermates.
claims.source: Furthermore, the vascular network was less intricate and had significantly fewer branching points in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos compared to wild-type littermates (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification data in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Many small vessels in E15.5 Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos lack a clear lumen and PECAM-1 immunosignals, representing retracted vessels.
claims.source: Interestingly, collagen IV immunostaining indicated that many small vessels in E15.5 Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos lacked a clear lumen and PECAM-1 immunosignals (see arrowheads in Figure 7C). They probably represent retracted vessels and were significantly more frequent in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos compared to wild-type, Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3+/+ and Fn1+/+;Itgb3-/- littermates (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 7C,D.

claims.claim: Small vessels in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos are often less covered by pericytes, with NG2-positive pericytes either detached or forming patchy aggregates on the vessel surface.
claims.source: Moreover, small vessels in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were often less covered by pericytes. Instead, NG2-positive pericytes were either detached or formed patchy aggregates on the vessel surface (see arrowheads in Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: The vessel wall coverage and stability are decreased in the Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos and probably contribute to their severe hemorrhages.
claims.source: Altogether, these observations indicate that the vessel wall coverage and stability are decreased in the Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos and probably contribute to their severe hemorrhages.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the vascular defects observed in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos.

claims.claim: Ablation of the Fn1 gene in mice arrests development at embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) due to defects in the formation of mesoderm and mesoderm-derived structures.
claims.source: Ablation of the Fn1 gene in mice, as well as the simultaneous ablations of the Itga5/Itgav integrin genes in mice arrests development at embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) due to defects in the formation of mesoderm and mesoderm-derived structures (George et al., 1993; Georges-Labouesse et al., 1996; Yang et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work (George et al., 1993; Georges-Labouesse et al., 1996; Yang et al., 1999).

claims.claim: The replacement of the FNIII10 RGD motif with RGE in mice affects mesoderm development, restricted to the vascular system and to the posterior region of the developing embryo.
claims.source: The replacement of the FNIII10 RGD motif with the RGE in mice also affects mesoderm development, although less severe and restricted to the vascular system and to the posterior region of the developing embryo (Takahashi et al., 2007; Girós et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work (Takahashi et al., 2007; Girós et al., 2011).

claims.claim: The RGE mutation is sufficient to abrogate α5β1 integrin function.
claims.source: Interestingly, these defects resemble those observed in Itga5-deficient mice indicating that the RGE mutation is sufficient to abrogate α5β1 integrin function and that the synergy site cannot compensate for a dysfunctional RGD motif.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by comparison to Itga5-deficient mice phenotypes.

claims.claim: The synergy site cannot compensate for a dysfunctional RGD motif.
claims.source: Interestingly, these defects resemble those observed in Itga5-deficient mice indicating that the RGE mutation is sufficient to abrogate α5β1 integrin function and that the synergy site cannot compensate for a dysfunctional RGD motif.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the phenotypic similarity between RGE mutant and Itga5-deficient mice.

claims.claim: The normal development of Fn1syn/syn mice excludes an essential role of the synergy site for α5 integrin function in vivo.
claims.source: Furthermore, the normal development of Fn1syn/syn mice also excludes an essential role of the synergy site for α5 integrin function in vivo (Grant et al., 1997; Krammer et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the normal development observed in Fn1syn/syn mice, with citations to prior hypotheses.

claims.claim: The absence of obvious 'α5β1-loss-of-function defects' in Fn1syn/syn mice indicates that the synergy site is probably dispensable to accelerate α5β1 integrin-FN binding.
claims.source: However, the absence of obvious 'α5β1-loss-of-function defects' (Yang et al., 1993) in Fn1syn/syn mice and the normal FN-binding on-rates of pKO-β1 cells in single-cell force spectroscopy experiments indicate that the synergy site is probably dispensable to accelerate α5β1 integrin-FN binding.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the normal development of Fn1syn/syn mice and single-cell force spectroscopy data, with a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: There is an unexpected, compensatory role between the FN synergy site and αvβ3 integrins for the vascular coverage by smooth muscle cells.
claims.source: We also demonstrate an unexpected, compensatory role between the FN synergy site and αvβ3 integrins for the vascular coverage by smooth muscle cells.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the severe vascular defects in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos.

claims.claim: High myosin II-induced forces generated by smooth muscle cells are only efficiently absorbed with either high αv-class integrin surface levels or a fully functional FN.
claims.source: Apparently, the high myosin II-induced forces generated by these cells are only efficiently absorbed with either high αv-class integrin surface levels or a fully functional FN.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the vascular smooth muscle cell defects in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos.

claims.claim: There is clear evidence for a compensatory role of the FN synergy site and αv-class integrins for cell spreading and FA maturation in vitro.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also find clear evidence for a compensatory role of the FN synergy site and αv-class integrins for cell spreading and FA maturation in vitro (Figure 8)
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the cell-based assays with different integrin-expressing cell lines, with reference to Figure 8.

claims.claim: Platelet adhesion to pFN, mediated by αIIbβ3 with contributions from α5β1 and other integrins, plays a critical role for hemostasis.
claims.source: It is well known that platelet adhesion to pFN, mediated by αIIbβ3 with contributions from α5β1 and other integrins, plays a critical role for hemostasis (Wang et al., 2014; Ni et al., 2003b).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work (Wang et al., 2014; Ni et al., 2003b).

claims.claim: The FN synergy site is critically important for the adhesion of wild type platelets in in vitro flow chamber settings.
claims.source: Our findings revealed that the FN synergy site is critically important for the adhesion of wild type platelets in in vitro flow chamber settings, while impaired spreading or defects under static adhesion only arise when αIIbβ3 expression is lost.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the flow chamber assay data with wild-type and Itgb3-/- platelets.

claims.claim: The synergy site plays a central role as soon as force is applied to the bonds between FN and platelet integrins.
claims.source: These findings indicate that the synergy site plays a central role as soon as force is applied to the bonds between FN and platelet integrins.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the differential effects of the synergy site mutation under static vs flow conditions.

claims.claim: The requirement of the synergy site for platelets to resist the shear forces of the blood flow provides a rational explanation for the prolonged bleeding times observed in Fn1syn/syn mice after tail tip excisions.
claims.source: This requirement of the synergy site for platelets to resist the shear forces of the blood flow also provides a rational explanation for the prolonged bleeding times observed in Fn1syn/syn mice after tail tip excisions.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and connects the in vitro flow chamber findings to the in vivo bleeding phenotype.

claims.claim: Murine platelets contain around 100 times more αIIbβ3 than α5β1 integrins.
claims.source: Since murine platelets contain around 100 times more αIIbβ3 than α5β1 integrins (Zeiler et al., 2014) the compensation of the entire αIIbβ3 pool by the minor α5β1-FNwt complexes underscores the fundamental role of the adhesion strengthening property of the synergy site in FN.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior published work (Zeiler et al., 2014).

claims.claim: The compensation of the entire αIIbβ3 pool by the minor α5β1-FNwt complexes underscores the fundamental role of the adhesion strengthening property of the synergy site in FN.
claims.source: Since murine platelets contain around 100 times more αIIbβ3 than α5β1 integrins (Zeiler et al., 2014) the compensation of the entire αIIbβ3 pool by the minor α5β1-FNwt complexes underscores the fundamental role of the adhesion strengthening property of the synergy site in FN.

results.result: Fn1syn/syn mice with a dysfunctional fibronectin synergy site are viable, fertile, and show normal organ morphology, blood vessel organization, and postnatal homeostasis, indicating that the synergy site is dispensable for development.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19 collectively demonstrate normal development and homeostasis in Fn1syn/syn mice through breeding data showing normal Mendelian ratios, histological analysis of multiple organs, and vascular immunostaining. The data converge to support the conclusion that the synergy site is not essential for development.

results.result: Fn1syn/syn mice exhibit mild bleeding defects characterized by prolonged bleeding time (7.27±1.71 min vs 4.64±1.50 min) and delayed thrombus formation (28.56±10.24 min vs 17.82±9.74 min) despite normal platelet counts and in vitro aggregation, demonstrating that the synergy site is required to stabilize platelet clots in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C28 provide comprehensive evidence from tail bleeding assays, arteriole occlusion experiments, and platelet characterization. The statistical significance (p<0.001) and consistent phenotype across multiple assays support the conclusion that the synergy site is critical for hemostasis under physiological stress.

results.result: The fibronectin synergy site is dispensable for FN fibril assembly but promotes the transition from nascent adhesions to mature focal adhesions, as demonstrated by delayed FA maturation and cell spreading on pFNsyn substrates in the first 30 minutes.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C35 are supported by immunofluorescence imaging, quantification of FA numbers and coverage, cell area measurements, and time-lapse microscopy. The data consistently show normal FN assembly but delayed FA maturation on pFNsyn, supporting the conclusion about the synergy site's role in adhesion maturation rather than initial binding.

results.result: Cells develop reduced adhesion strength on synergy site-deficient FN, with τ50 values decreased by 16% on full-length pFNsyn and 43% on FNIII7-10syn fragments compared to wild-type, indicating force-dependent adhesion strengthening requires the synergy site.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 are supported by spinning disk assay data showing quantitative reductions in adhesion strength. The greater effect on fragments vs full-length FN suggests additional stabilizing interactions in full-length protein, supporting the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: The synergy site enables force-dependent strengthening of α5β1-FN bonds, as demonstrated by crosslinking experiments showing that spinning force increases α5 integrin-FN crosslinking on pFNwt but not pFNsyn.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 are supported by chemical crosslinking assays with and without applied force. The differential response to spinning between pFNwt and pFNsyn provides direct evidence for synergy site-dependent bond tensioning, supporting the catch-bond mechanism.

results.result: Fibroblasts on pFNsyn show 54% reduced pY397-FAK phosphorylation compared to pFNwt while pY861-FAK remains unchanged, indicating that cells attached to pFNsyn perceive insufficient information about substrate stiffness.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are supported by Western blot quantification and appropriate controls (pY861-FAK). The selective reduction in force-dependent FAK phosphorylation with citation to prior work on FAK as a rigidity sensor supports the mechanistic interpretation about substrate sensing.

results.result: αv-class integrins compensate for the absent synergy site during cell adhesion and spreading, as pKO-β1 cells (expressing only α5β1) show severe defects on pFNsyn while pKO-αv and pKO-αv/β1 cells spread normally.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 are supported by systematic comparison of cell lines with defined integrin expression patterns. The differential behavior of pKO-β1 vs pKO-αv/β1 cells on pFNsyn provides strong evidence for compensatory mechanisms between integrin classes.

results.result: The FN synergy site does not accelerate the initial binding rate of α5β1 integrins to FN, as single-cell force spectroscopy shows no difference in binding probability between pFNwt and pFNsyn, and αvβ3 integrins show 3-fold higher affinity for FN-RGD than α5β1.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by single-cell force spectroscopy with short contact times (≈50 ms) designed to measure initial binding events. The lack of difference between pFNwt and pFNsyn contradicts prior hypotheses about synergy site effects on binding kinetics, supporting a role in adhesion strengthening rather than initial contact.

results.result: Compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- mice show embryonic lethality between E15.5 and E16.5, with only 1 of 335 expected offspring surviving to P21, while heterozygous Itgb3 mice show normal distribution, indicating one β3 integrin allele is sufficient for development.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 are supported by extensive breeding data in Table 1 showing Mendelian ratios at different developmental stages. The dramatic deviation from expected ratios (1 vs 38 expected survivors) and normal distribution of heterozygotes provide strong evidence for genetic interaction between the synergy site and β3 integrins.

results.result: Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos display severe hemorrhages and lymphatic vessel defects starting at E11.5/12.5, with dilated Lyve1-positive lymphatic vessels covered with ectopic α-SMA-positive cells and filled with erythroblasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by whole embryo imaging and immunostaining data showing hemorrhages and abnormal lymphatic vessel morphology. The specificity of the phenotype to compound mutants (not seen in single mutants) supports the genetic interaction.

results.result: The FN synergy site is critical for platelet adhesion under shear flow, with wild-type platelet adhesion to pFNsyn reduced 10-fold under flow, and Itgb3-/- platelets failing to spread on pFNsyn (3.8 μm²) while showing partial spreading on pFNwt (8.9 μm²), demonstrating that α5β1 integrins partially compensate for αIIbβ3 loss in a synergy site-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C76 are supported by comprehensive platelet spreading and flow chamber assays with appropriate controls (collagen). The quantitative measurements and differential effects under static vs flow conditions provide strong evidence for force-dependent synergy site function in platelets.

results.result: Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos show severe vascular defects including tortuous vessels with irregular smooth muscle coverage, significantly fewer branching points, increased retracted vessels lacking lumen, and detached pericytes, indicating decreased vessel wall stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are supported by immunostaining and quantification of vascular parameters at E15.5. The multiple converging lines of evidence (vessel morphology, branching, pericyte coverage) support the conclusion about compromised vascular stability in compound mutants.

results.result: There is an unexpected compensatory role between the FN synergy site and αvβ3 integrins for vascular smooth muscle cell coverage, with high myosin II-induced forces requiring either high αv-class integrin levels or a fully functional FN synergy site.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by the severe vascular phenotype in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos and in vitro cell spreading data. The genetic interaction and cell-based mechanistic studies converge to support the compensatory mechanism, though the myosin II force interpretation is somewhat inferential.

results.result: The normal development of Fn1syn/syn mice excludes an essential role of the synergy site for α5β1 integrin function in vivo and indicates the synergy site is dispensable for accelerating α5β1 integrin-FN binding rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by the normal development phenotype and single-cell force spectroscopy data. This result effectively refutes prior hypotheses about synergy site function in guiding initial integrin-FN binding, representing an important negative result.

results.result: The FN synergy site is critical when external forces exceed a threshold or when αvβ3 integrin levels decrease below a critical level, as demonstrated by mild defects in Fn1syn/syn mice that become severe with additional β3 integrin loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C5 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the comprehensive in vivo and in vitro data. The force-dependence and integrin compensation mechanisms are well-documented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The synergy site is dispensable for initial α5β1 contact with RGD but essential to re-enforce α5β1/αIIbβ3 binding to FN.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 summarize key mechanistic findings supported by single-cell force spectroscopy (initial binding), crosslinking assays, and spinning disk experiments (adhesion strengthening). The distinction between initial contact and bond reinforcement is well-supported.

results.result: FN content in platelets from Fn1syn/syn mice is reduced to 70% while plasma FN levels remain normal (316.1±31.0 vs 318.7±24.1 μg/ml).
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 are supported by Western blot quantification of platelet lysates and plasma. The selective reduction in platelet FN with normal plasma levels suggests impaired αIIbβ3-mediated uptake into α-granules, consistent with synergy site function.

results.result: Adhesion of Fn1-KO cells to pFNwt and pFNsyn begins around 3 min after seeding and increases similarly over time.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 is supported by adhesion assay data showing no difference in initial adhesion kinetics. This supports the conclusion that the synergy site does not affect initial cell-substrate contact.

results.result: Vessels in the trunk of Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos show normal sprouting at E11.5.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is supported by PECAM-1 immunostaining of whole mount embryos. This temporal specificity helps define when the vascular defects emerge in compound mutants.

results.result: Background information on fibronectin structure, the RGD motif, and synergy site, including their integrin binding specificities and effects on cell spreading, FN assembly, and platelet adhesion in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C15 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These provide necessary context for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: Prior work shows that Fn1 gene ablation arrests development at E8.5, RGD to RGE mutation affects vascular development, and the RGE mutation is sufficient to abrogate α5β1 function while the synergy site cannot compensate for a dysfunctional RGD motif.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 accurately summarize prior published work with appropriate citations. The interpretation that the synergy site cannot compensate for RGD dysfunction is logical based on the cited phenotypes.

results.result: The FN synergy site is critically important for wild-type platelet adhesion under flow conditions, plays a central role when force is applied to FN-integrin bonds, and provides a rational explanation for prolonged bleeding times in Fn1syn/syn mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 represent interpretive conclusions well-supported by the platelet adhesion and flow chamber data. The connection between in vitro force-dependent adhesion and in vivo bleeding phenotype is logical and well-argued.

results.result: Murine platelets contain ~100 times more αIIbβ3 than α5β1 integrins, yet the minor α5β1-FNwt complexes can compensate for the entire αIIbβ3 pool, underscoring the fundamental role of the synergy site's adhesion strengthening property.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96 are supported by citation to prior work on integrin levels and the current platelet adhesion data. The quantitative comparison effectively highlights the potency of synergy site-mediated adhesion strengthening.

results.result: The separation of the primary lymphatic sac from the cardinal vein is driven by platelet adhesion and aggregation, and platelet functions are severely compromised in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos due to loss of both αIIbβ3-mediated binding and α5β1-mediated adhesion strengthening.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 connect prior knowledge about lymphatic development to the observed phenotype. The hypothesis about compromised platelet function is well-supported by the in vitro platelet data and the lymphatic vessel defects observed.

results.result: Background information on FN structure, assembly, plasma FN function, integrin-mediated uptake, FAK phosphorylation, and the Itgb3-null mouse model.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C111 represent established knowledge with appropriate citations. These provide necessary mechanistic context for interpreting the experimental findings.
